Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for Bangladesh's reply. The floodlights are on and the cloud cover remains over the stadium as the two umpires and players make their way out to the middle. After taking a blow to the helmet while batting, Mohammad Rizwan has not taken the field, with Sarfaraz Ahmed stepping in as his replacement. Out walk Zakir Hasan and Shadman Islam to open the innings for Bangladesh. They have around 25 minutes to contend with before the Tea break. Mir Hamza is at the top of his mark and he is raring to go. Off we go...
... FOURTH INNINGS ...

Right then, chasing 185 runs will be far from easy, especially considering Bangladesh's struggles in the first innings when they were reduced to 26-6. The memory of that inning may still linger. As they did in the first innings, Pakistan will be eager to strike early and put the visitors on the back foot right from the start. Back in a bit for the chase.

A masterful bowling effort from Bangladesh to bowl out Pakistan for 172. Hasan Mahmud, the chief wrecker, with a five-wicket haul, has become the first Bangladeshi pacer to take five wickets or more in Pakistan. Bangladesh now need 185 runs to win the Test match and seal a rare away series victory. Pakistan were reeling at 65/5 when Babar Azam was dismissed, but Mohammad Rizwan mounted a decent fightback, counterattacking to score 43. Agha Salman played the supporting role alongside Rizwan and, after his dismissal, carried on batting with Pakistan's tail. He used his smarts to farm the strike and unleashed big shots to keep the scoreboard ticking, but just as it was beginning to frustrate Bangladesh, they wrapped up the innings.

OUT! TAKEN! Hasan Mahmud drops the ball short from around the wicket, angling into the left-hander. Mir Hamza, expecting the ball to bounce more, is uncomfortable at the crease and looks to flick the ball, getting a faint inside edge onto the pads. The ball lobs up straight to Mehidy Hasan at second slip who grabs it well. Huge shout and the umpire raises his finger. Mir Hamza takes the review. UltraEdge shows a spike as the ball passes the bat, but the bat is simultaneously making contact with the pad. With no conclusive evidence to overturn the on-field decision, the third umpire sticks to the on-field call. Pakistan end with 172 on the board with a lead of 184 runs.

Pakistan's physio is having a chat with the match officials, likely discussing the situation with Mohammad Rizwan who took a blow to the helmet in the morning session. With the tail to follow, a lot will depend on this pair to help Pakistan reach a challenging total. For Bangladesh, the key will be to return with the same intensity to break this stand and open up one end. Thankfully, the weather has held up so far, and let’s hope it continues to cooperate for the rest of the day. The Test has already delivered plenty of excitement, and we can expect more thrilling action as it progresses. The second session will commence at 7.40 am GMT. See you then. Cheers!

Things could have been even worse if Shadman Islam had not dropped Mohammad Rizwan on the very first ball he faced. Rizwan, undeterred by a blow to the helmet, remained proactive and kept the scoreboard ticking. Although he showed signs of feeling the after-effects of the blow, Rizwan chose to continue until the break. Pakistan scored 108 runs in the first session at the loss of 4 wickets and they currently lead by 129 runs.

End of yet another fascinating session of Test cricket! The session didn’t begin as Bangladesh would have hoped, but they’ll be pleased with where the Test stands at the end of the first session. Shan Masood and Saim Ayub got Pakistan off to a bright start, looking largely untroubled until their dismissals. Once both set batters fell, Pakistan’s innings took a rapid downturn. Nahid Rana turned up the heat, and the hosts slumped from 62-3 to 81-6.
Pushed through, full and on the pads, Mohammad Rizwan gets his bat out in front of the pads and defends it out. That will be LUNCH on Day 4!

He admits he was nervous at the start, but Mehidy Hasan's encouragement helped calm his nerves. Litton mentions that after getting hit on the elbow early on, Mehidy took the initiative, and as he began to feel better after the second session, he started playing his shots more confidently.

Khurram Shahzad is in for a flash interview. He shares that the new ball is his strength, something he’s well-versed with from his domestic cricket experience. Adds that he always tries to hit the right areas and acknowledges that momentum shifts that are part of Test cricket. States that he always looks to keep the stumps in play. When asked about his personal favorite among the six wickets he took, Shahzad mentions that he particularly enjoyed dismissing Najmul Hossain Shanto.

He notes that spin has troubled Pakistan, with their footwork appearing tentative, while Bangladesh have been more decisive in their approach against spin. Compton opines that Pakistan will need to be clear in their decision-making to counter spin effectively.

As we move into Day 4, Pakistan's top order will have to step up and build a substantial lead. Shan Masood, Babar Azam, and Mohammad Rizwan will be under immense pressure to deliver, especially after a disappointing start. Bangladesh, on the other hand, will be buoyed by their strong finish on Day 3 and will aim to keep the momentum going. With both teams having shown moments of brilliance and vulnerability, Day 4 promises to be decisive in this Test match. Rain is expected today and on Day 5 as well but let's hope that it stays away. Stay tuned.

Litton Das, however, was not done yet. He continued his innings with determination and reached his fourth Test century, a knock that held the Bangladesh innings together. Alongside Hasan Mahmud, Das added a further 69 runs for the ninth wicket, frustrating the Pakistani bowlers who were searching for a quick end to the innings. Eventually, Salman Ali Agha managed to dismiss Das for a valiant 138, breaking the stubborn 69-run partnership. Bangladesh's innings concluded at 262 runs in 78.4 overs, just 12 runs shy of Pakistan's first-innings total. The final few overs of the day were crucial, and Pakistan needed to avoid further setbacks. However, Bangladesh struck early, with Abdullah Shafique falling, chasing a wide delivery before the nightwatchman Khurram Shahzad fell on what ended up being the final ball of the day.

But cricket, especially in the longest format, often throws up surprises, and Day 3 was no exception. Litton Das and Mehidy Hasan orchestrated a phenomenal rescue act for Bangladesh, demonstrating resilience and composure under pressure. Their partnership for the seventh wicket, worth 165 runs, was a record-breaking feat. For the first time in Test cricket history, a seventh-wicket stand crossed 150 runs after the first six wickets fell for under 30. Mehidy played a crucial role with his well-crafted 78 before finally succumbing to Shahzad just before the Tea break.

Day 3 began with Bangladesh at 10/0, facing a tricky task after two overs the previous evening. However, the morning session was all about Pakistan's bowlers, particularly Khurram Shahzad, who unleashed a sensational spell. Bangladesh's top order crumbled, unable to cope with the relentless attack, and they found themselves reeling at 26/6 by the 12th over. It seemed as though Pakistan would run through the visitors' batting lineup, potentially enforcing a follow-on and taking a commanding position in the match.

Earlier in the day, Pakistan staged a remarkable turnaround as Khurram Shahzad and Mir Hamza dismantled the Bangladesh top 6 within the first 11 overs. With Bangladesh at a precarious 26/6, their record-lowest team total of 43 in Tests seemed under threat. However, Litton Das and Mehidy Hasan staged a marathon recovery with a 165-run stand. Their partnership was brought to an end by Khurram Shahzad who went on to scalp another in his following over. Never before in the history of Test cricket had there been a 7th wicket partnership of 150 or more runs after the first 6 wickets had fallen for 30 runs or fewer. It was indeed a monumental effort from Litton Das and Mehidy Hasan.

At the start of the third session, trailing by 81 runs with only two wickets remaining, Bangladesh's hopes hinged on Litton Das. He leveraged his experience while batting with Hasan Mahmud, and edged Bangladesh closer to parity with his 4th Test ton. As the new ball approached, he took on Agha Salman but fell in the process. Nahid Rana was unable to add to the score, leaving Bangladesh with 262 on the board and Pakistan holding a slender 12-run lead. The Test was left hanging in the balance as a one-inning shootout. Pakistan's openers faced a challenging 20-minute period to see out the remaining overs. Abdullah Shafique's difficult Test continued, and in the final over of the day,  the nightwatchman Khurram Shahzad was dismissed by a stunning delivery from Hasan Mahmud, leaving Pakistan with 8 wickets in hand and a 21-run lead.

End of a fantastic day of Test cricket! This is why we love the format, don't we? The dramatic ebbs and flows have kept us on the edge of our seats, and it continues to deliver moments of pure excitement. While the first session went Pakistan's way, the next couple of sessions saw a fight back from Bangladesh, leaving the Test delicately poised at the end of Day 3.
